v.why: Adding a direct input-to-output shortcut gains much more when it fills an empty edge than when it replaces a conv.
Replacing a 3x3 conv with a skip discards learned capacity, so the edit helps less or hurts.
Filling a removed final-hop edge with a conv recovers far more than upgrading an existing op.
Parallel inputs to node 3 show diminishing returns when edge 5 already has a strong conv.
A second strong conv into the output node is partly redundant with edge 5.
With a strong direct 0->3 conv, upgrading the 2->3 path adds less.
Substitutable parallel convs into node 3 give diminishing marginal returns.
A direct skip already supplies the gradient and feature shortcut, so the conv upgrade on edge 5 matters less.
With edge 2 removed, edge 0 reaches the output only through edge 4, so it is closer to a bottleneck-free dead end.
Edge 1 only feeds node 2, which is useless to the output if edge 5 is none, so upgrading it does nothing.
Edge 2 also feeds only node 2, so upgrading it is wasted when edge 5 is removed.
Removing edge 4 forces edge 0's signal through the longer 1->2->3 route, which weakens its benefit.
Deleting edge 2 is harmless when edge 5 is already none, since node 2 is dead anyway.
Deleting edge 1 costs nothing when its downstream edge 5 is absent.
With edge 4 gone, removing edge 0 cuts less of the output signal, so it hurts less than when edge 4 is live.
Removing the 2->3 path hurts less when a strong direct 0->3 conv remains.
A strong parallel direct path makes edge 4 dispensable, so deleting it hurts less.
Dropping the direct edge hurts less when the 2->3 path carries a strong conv.
Removing an existing skip shortcut hurts trainability, which is worse than removing other ops.
Pooling over an empty edge adds a path, whereas replacing a conv or skip loses capacity.
Two parallel skips into the output are redundant, so the second adds less.
A skip on edge 4 duplicates the identity role already served by edge 3.
Both edges feed node 2 as substitutes, so a second strong conv has diminishing returns.
Restoring an absent final-hop edge with any conv gives a large gain compared with swapping ops.
Edge 2 already provides strong input to node 2 through a parallel route, so edge 1 is partly redundant.
A strong conv on the parallel route into node 2 reduces the marginal value of strengthening edge 0.
A skip on edge 5 already provides a gradient shortcut, so the added skip on edge 3 brings less.
Replacing a conv with a pool throws away learnable capacity, which is worse than pooling over weaker ops.
Restoring a missing intermediate edge with a conv matters more than upgrading an existing one.
